Analysis

Hit Rate

Per-workload cache hit rates reveal the true picture. With per-table metrics (separate keyspaces for hot and scan workloads), we can see:

  • Hot HR: How well the cache protects frequently-accessed data under scan pressure
  • Scan HR: Expected to be near-zero since the scan set (500k rows) far exceeds cache capacity
  • Combined HR: The aggregate masks the per-workload difference

Tail Latency

The most significant difference appears in tail latency:

  • Large window (LRU-like): scan entries flood the window, causing occasional eviction of hot entries that must then be re-read from disk — visible as p99+ spikes
  • Small window (frequency-dominant): the Count-Min Sketch frequency filter blocks most scan entries from entering the SLRU cache, protecting hot data

Why differences are smaller than simulation

  • Uniform access pattern: hash(i) % N distributes reads uniformly, unlike Zipfian where a few keys are much hotter. Uniform means all keys have similar frequency, reducing the advantage of frequency-based admission.
  • Cache overhead: Real entries carry metadata; partition-level caching differs from fixed-size slot simulation.
  • Background activity: Compaction, memtable flushes, and other ScyllaDB internals affect cache behaviour.

Conclusion

Even with uniform access patterns and real-world overhead, smaller W-TinyLFU window sizes provide measurably better scan resistance, particularly in tail latency. The default 1% window is a good choice for most workloads.
